about: Electronics Design Project 1 (ELEC40006) is the compulsory year-long team project for first-year EEE and EIE students at Imperial, worth 7.5 ECTS. Teams take a new client brief each year (a system combining analogue sensing, digital control and a computer interface) from requirements through design and testing to a demonstrated prototype, supported by an introduction to systems engineering, compulsory professional skills workshops and bookable expert consultations. The department's descriptor (last revised December 2024) lists a client meeting and presentation (20%), a design process and technical solution report (40%) and a demonstration and interview (40%), with completion of Workshops 1–7 as a must-pass element. As a project module it has no fixed syllabus, so this is a guide to how it works and how to prepare.
topics: What the project is and how it runs
Systems engineering: requirements, specifications and test plans
Teamwork, documentation, cost and presenting to the client

notes.body:
Electronics Design Project 1 (ELEC40006) is the first-year group design project for Imperial's EEE (and EIE) students. It runs across all three terms and is worth 7.5 ECTS. Unlike a lecture module there is no fixed syllabus to revise: you learn by designing, building and testing a real system in a team.

What the department's descriptor (last revised December 2024) says about the project
- Each year there is a new brief, set by a "client", for a system that combines analogue sensing, digital control and a computer interface. The details change annually, so do not rely on previous years' solutions.
- The project draws on the main topics studied in the first year, and asks you to integrate analogue, digital and software design in one system.
- It starts with an introduction to systems engineering: how complex systems are designed, built and operated.
- The design work itself is largely student-led: research, planning and implementation, all the way from the client brief to demonstrating a working prototype.
- There are compulsory professional skills workshops (two in each of the Autumn and Spring terms and a few in the Summer term) on non-technical skills such as teamwork and report writing.
- You can book consultations with technical experts throughout the project, and there are formative engineering-design team-based learning classes.
- A teaching laboratory is timetabled for the project every working day.

Study time
The descriptor allocates 187.5 hours in total, of which only about 36 are scheduled teaching (lectures, group teaching and lab sessions); the rest, about 151.5 hours, is independent and team work. Planning your own time is therefore part of the challenge.

What you should come away able to do
The learning outcomes are about process as much as product: capturing and analysing requirements and turning them into specifications; applying theory and lab skills within practical constraints; integrating analogue, digital and software design; working effectively in a team and evaluating your own and the team's performance; writing and running a test plan; communicating through a written report and a demonstration; and planning and recording your own learning as a basis for continuing professional development.

How to get started well
- Read the brief several times and list every requirement, including implied ones (power source, size, cost limit, safety).
- Agree team roles early, but make sure everyone understands the whole system.
- Book an early consultation once you have a concept, not when something has already gone wrong.

notes.h: Assessment and what examiners look for
notes.body:
The department's module descriptor (last revised December 2024) gives the following assessment. Check the current version on the department's site, as details can change.

Components
- Client meeting and presentation (practical): 20%.
- Design process and technical solution report (coursework): 40%.
- Demonstration and interview (practical): 40%.
- Workshops 1–7, completion of activities: 0% of the mark, but must be passed (100% completion required). Missing workshops can therefore stop you passing the module even if the technical work is excellent.

The overall pass mark is 40%, with numeric grading. Because the project depends on teamwork, there is no in-session resit; a failed module is retaken in the following Summer term.

How to prepare for each part
Client meeting and presentation
- Treat the client as someone who needs to be convinced, not as an examiner who knows the answer. Show that you understood the brief, how you turned it into measurable specifications, your chosen architecture and your plan.
- Keep slides simple: block diagrams, key numbers and decisions with reasons.
- Rehearse timing and agree who answers which kinds of question.

Report
- The report is about the design process and the technical solution, so record decisions as you go: options considered, why you chose one, test evidence.
- Structure it so a reader can follow from requirements to specification, design, test results and evaluation against the specification. Be honest about what did not work and why.
- Use figures with captions, units on every axis, and refer to them in the text.

Demonstration and interview
- Demonstrate against your specification and test plan, not just "it works". Have test cases ready that show each requirement being met.
- Every team member should be able to explain any subsystem, because interview questions may go to anyone.
- Prepare for things going wrong on the day: spare batteries, a known-good configuration, and a recorded fallback if the live demo fails partway.

Workshops
- Attend and complete every activity; these are the must-pass part. Some workshop activities are themselves assessed as part of completion.

notes.h: Systems engineering: from brief to specification to test plan
notes.body:
The project opens with an introduction to systems engineering. The core idea is simple: before designing anything, define exactly what the system must do and how you will prove it does it.

Requirements versus specifications
- A requirement states what the client needs, often in their own words: "the device must detect the target from across a room".
- A specification is a measurable, testable statement derived from it: "detects a 1 kHz signal at 3 m with at least 95% success over 20 trials".
- Good specifications are specific, measurable, achievable within the time and budget, relevant to the brief, and testable. If you cannot describe the test, the specification is not finished.
- Separate functional requirements (what it does) from non-functional ones (cost, power, size, reliability, safety, usability).

System architecture
- Break the system into subsystems with clear interfaces: for a typical brief, a sensing front end (analogue), signal processing or control (digital or microcontroller/FPGA), and a computer interface (software).
- Define each interface precisely: voltage ranges, data formats, timing, connectors. Most integration failures happen at interfaces, not inside subsystems.
- Assign subsystems to people so work proceeds in parallel, but keep an interface document that everyone agrees.

The V-model way of thinking
Design moves down from system requirements to subsystem design to components; verification moves back up, testing components, then subsystems, then the integrated system against the original requirements. Each level of design should have a matching level of test planned from the start.

Writing a test plan
For each specification, write:
- the test purpose (which specification it checks);
- the set-up and equipment;
- the procedure, in steps someone else could follow;
- the pass/fail criterion with numbers;
- a place for the measured result and any notes.
Run subsystem tests before integration, then system tests after. Record failures as well as successes: they are evidence of a sound process.

Iterate
Early prototypes on a breadboard or simulation (for example a circuit simulator, or Quartus for digital logic) reveal problems cheaply. Update the specification, design and test plan as you learn, and record why.

notes.h: Working as a team, documenting, managing cost and presenting
notes.body:
The descriptor lists working effectively individually and in a team, allocating workload and evaluating your own and the team's performance as learning outcomes in their own right. It also expects you to plan and record your own learning.

Team organisation
- Agree a team charter early: meeting times, how decisions are made, how disagreements are resolved, and expectations for communication response times.
- Allocate roles (for example coordinator, subsystem leads, documentation lead) but rotate or overlap so knowledge is not held by one person.
- Hold short regular meetings with an agenda and written actions (who, what, by when). Review actions at the next meeting.
- If a teammate is struggling or absent, raise it early and constructively, and if it continues, speak to the module team.

Planning
- Work back from fixed dates (client presentation, report deadline, demonstration) to set internal milestones, leaving a buffer for integration and testing, which always takes longer than expected.
- A simple Gantt chart or task board, kept up to date, makes progress visible.

Documentation
- Keep a shared logbook or repository: design decisions with reasons, schematics, code with version control, test results with dates. This becomes the raw material for the report.
- Label every schematic and code version so the build on the bench matches the documents.

Cost management
- Keep a bill of materials with part numbers, quantities and unit costs, and track it against any budget in the brief.
- Order parts early and have alternatives in mind; lead times can stall a project.

Presenting and communicating
- Tailor each communication to its audience: the client wants to know that their needs will be met; technical assessors want evidence and reasoning.
- In the report and presentation, use block diagrams to show the whole system before details.
- Reflect honestly in your personal development record: what you learned, what you would do differently, and evidence of your contribution.

questions.q: According to the module descriptor (last revised December 2024), which ELEC40006 component carries 0% of the mark but must be passed?
options: Design process and technical solution report
questions.why: Completion of the professional skills workshops is weighted 0% but is the module's must-pass element. The client meeting and presentation is worth 20%, the report 40% and the demonstration and interview 40%; these carry marks, and the descriptor does not list any of them as must-pass components, so mixing up weighting with must-pass status leads to choosing one of them.

questions.q: Which of these is a well-formed, testable specification rather than a requirement?
options: The sensor detects a 1 kHz tone at 3 m in at least 19 of 20 trials
The system must be easy for the client to use
The detector should have a long range
questions.why: Only the tone-detection statement gives a measurable quantity, a condition and a pass/fail criterion, so it can be checked by a test. 'Work reliably' is a requirement with no measure of reliability attached. 'Easy to use' is a usability requirement that needs a measurable criterion (e.g. time to complete a task) before it becomes a specification. 'Long range' names a quantity but gives no number, so there is no pass/fail threshold.

questions.q: A client asks for 'a device that detects when someone enters a room and reports it to a laptop'. Turn this into three measurable specifications and describe a test for one of them.
markScheme: Three specifications, each with a measurable quantity and threshold (e.g. detection range, detection rate, latency to laptop, battery life)
Specifications cover different subsystems (sensing, processing, interface)
Test describes set-up, procedure and number of trials
Clear numerical pass/fail criterion linked to the specification
questions.modelAnswer: Possible specifications: (1) detects a person walking through a 1 m wide doorway in at least 95% of 40 trials; (2) the laptop displays an 'entry' message within 1 s of detection; (3) runs for at least 8 hours from its battery. Test for (2): place the device at the doorway connected to the laptop running the interface; have a person walk through 20 times; record the time of crossing (e.g. with a video showing both the doorway and the laptop screen) and the time the message appears. Pass if every one of the 20 latencies is 1 s or less; record each measurement and any failures.
